questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The philosophy programme offered at Sorbonne University, and the possibility to improve my french, and lastly also because of the parisian culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Sorbonne University had sent e-mails that were quite detailed, but they always came a bit late, so it was hard not to be a little anxious if something had gone wrong.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were two different erasmus meetings, one general and one that was philosophy-specific which was quite detailed and thorough. Also it helped me a lot, that I have already studied there one semester during my BA-studies, so I knew my way around their particularities.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was O.K as I was willing to pay the extra price to go through a rental agency, but it wasn't easy to find a good one.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That it's way better than living on the small student housing offered at Clignancourt, but that rent in Paris is expensive (it should be possible to find a room in the 700-900€ range, and a studio apartment in the 800-1300€ range).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I was sent a link to a google sheets document where I had to write which courses I wanted to take.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can go to the philosophy office and ask the people there.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the ones I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Go to the erasmus meetings, and stay in contact with others who are going on exchange in that department, as Sorbonne sometimes mix up mail addresses. One of my friends did for example not receive all the official mails for some reason.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the level on most courses to be sufficiently high, while not too difficult to follow if you spend a normal time on studying.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is quite different in a lot of positive ways. It is more "old-school", meaning that professors usually have prepared a lecture that they give which is quite like a manuscript that they have prepared, that is usually complicated, which means that if you are well prepared you can get a lot out of it, and if you are less prepared you still learn something. What I'm getting at is that it seems that they don't focus so much on pedagogics or making sure that everyone is on the same page, but give an interesting lecture that draws on a lot of different material in order to make points about the given topic. As such the courses are usually way more topic-oriented where the professor is trying to give their own take or reading of a topic through incorporation of a lot of different sources. For me that makes the lectures more interesting because they take you through a line of thought which is similar to philosophical work, which is a bit different from the lectures that are usually given at UCPH where the focus is more that we should understand a specific text or idea for each lecture, which gives the lectures more of introductory feel. That said this more "old-school" approach has its downsides in that it is not clear what the students are supposed to read, but once you get used to this way of studying where you can more freely choose which texts you want to read, it is quite motivational. Another thing that I like which is different is that professors often encourage you to read books, rather than just academic papers, which I find more engaging as this gives you incitement to get deeper into the philosophers that are discussed in the specific course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Philosophy of Physics 
Temporalities of works of art
What is phenomenological in Hegel's 'Phenomenology of Spirit'
'Phenomenology of Perception' by Merleau-Ponty
System and history in german idealism - methodology of history of philosophy
Lastly I also took a french language course on C1 level.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I especially can recommend the more history-oriented philosophy courses (Phenomenology of Perception, and System and History), but also the metaphysics course about Hegel's Phenomenoogy of spirit. Lastly I can recommend to try a course on the philosophy of art, to try to make amends for the fact that aesthetics are not on the study programme in UCPH.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Electricity bill from my apartment was way higher than expected due to electric heating and bad insulation.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Books are very cheap. Food and drinks outside are generally cheaper than DK, while groceries are about the same. Transportation is not too bad if you are willing to bike on the public bike service.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I didn't enroll in any but I know that there are some free sport activites you can join which I heard are quite nice actually. Most museums and the like are free in Paris if you are under 26 and a student.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I can't tell as I didn't participate in any at the university.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Museums, because they might be free if you are young enough and there are so many good ones. 
Also going to vernissages for the galleries as there are usually some free drinks and you get to see what new or upcoming artists are working on. 
Visiting all the well-equipped and weird antiquity stores as well as second-hand book shops.
In general enjoying a cheap coffee or wine on the cafés.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be shy, although I didn't really socialize that much with the local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language barrier.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The lively streets and cafés.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be careful with following the procedures that you receive in e-mail from Sorbonne, but also don't hesitate to write them an e-mail if you are suspecting that they forgot to send you some important information.
Don't take too many courses, as it can be hard to make a good schedule and have time to read as well, or supply with a french course as they have a lighter work-load per ECTS point.
Practice your hand-writing.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get accustomed to writing by hand by taking notes by hand as well, most exams in the philosophy department are written in hand.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Finishing the exams and feeling that I did a good job. And making friends with other exchange students.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Exams.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
